question: can inference-level resolution (LLM maintenance pass + retrieval filtering) resolve implicit invalidation that rule-based ranking could not?
design: After seeding each B1 scenario, a maintenance pass (memplex/premise_resolution.py) groups memory pairs, asks glm-5.3-flash whether the later supersedes the earlier, and stamps the loser with premise_superseded in its namespace AND its referenced raw paragraphs. Retrieval filters stamped nodes from every leg (FTS, BM25, vector, paragraph). MEMPLEX_PREMISE_RESOLVE=0 restores the unresolved baseline.
findings: The MECHANISM works: resolved went 0 to 2 (the target was >0), and stale_reuse dropped 16pp (0.44 to 0.28). When the LLM correctly identifies the supersession pair, the retrieval filter removes the stale value from every surface - verified end-to-end (Berlin disappears after the pass).

The BOTTLENECK is detection accuracy, not architecture: glm-5.3-flash stamped only ~3 of 8 true pairs (conservative). The improved prompt (explicit supersession patterns) improved detection but also increased false positives (neither 5/25 - both sides filtered in some scenarios).

The retrieval filtering required four surface patches: FTS results, BM25 facts/preferences, vector leg documents, and the raw paragraph pool (both BM25 and vector). Each had its own filter point; missing any one lets the stale value resurface through that leg.

Full B1 resolution needs a stronger judge model for the pair audit (glm-5.3 full, not flash) or a per-domain prompt library. The infrastructure is complete and the flag is production-shaped (MEMPLEX_PREMISE_RESOLVE=1 default on, =0 to disable).
honest_reading: n=25; resolved 2 is above the 0-target but well short of saturation. The neither=5 cases (both filtered) are the false-positive cost of the permissive topic gate plus an eager LLM. Directional evidence is solid; the remaining work is model/prompt quality, not architecture.
